Author: @AndrewMakesPuns
Content:
The ethics of this are interesting. On the one hand, they cause immense suffering, especially in areas that havent had them before. Theyre also not harmed directly, but have their bloodlines eliminated (obv a human would still find this horrible, but I dont think we know if the flies have that concept).

On the other hand, we are still comitting genocide - which again idk if they'd care about that concept, but still. Also is the suffering of that genocide greater or lesser than that of their victims? Thirdly, I doubt theyre particularly aware that theyre causing harm, theyre just doing what presumably feels right. And lastly, even if they are purely parasites, do we know if they play a role in lessening the numbers of one of their target species or in providing a food source or other role to another species? And if not, just because we deem a species 'ecologically useless', because we have a scientific understanding of ecology, does that mean theyre okay to eliminate? What if we're wrong - the cost is unfathomably steep - thats why we dont have the death penalty in a lot of countries anymore. Is it fair to judge a species based on concepts only (as far as we know) used by humans? Have we even the right to eliminate species? How does the failure to eradicate and wall-breaks affect the balance of suffering?

Thank you for listening to my TED Talk

Content:
🤔
This was a fascinating vido... But I can't help but feel uneasy. We're releasing radioactive flies into nature to fight other flies, and it's presented as a perfect solution. But what about the rest of the food web? Dead or alive, these flies don’t just disappear... They're eaten by birds, insects, fungi, maybe even plants, crops. By definition... Biomagnification is the process by which the concentration of a toxic substance (like heavy metals, pesticides, or radioactive elements) increases at each successive level of the food chain. Radiation doesn’t stay in one place; it travels through everything that consumes it.

And then I saw that friendly animated bird at the end of the video... acting very human. 😅 Maybe it's already had a few of those flies. 

Science can be powerful, but maybe we should be cautious before declaring victory over nature... Only to find we've doomed ourselves in the process.😐

Author: @randykayser4145
Content:
It seems pretty irresponsible to advocate for this level of biological systems engineering. This especially goes for a goal which seems to primarily protect the interests of the cattle industry - an industry which is frequently described as a climatological nightmare. I have to say, it really floored me that there wasn't a single line in this whole video that even considered that this process might have drawbacks. 


Here is a drawback which screamed at me for essentially the whole video: what if we thought of these parasites as fulfilling a biological niche in the particular biome of a tropical rainforest? What would that niche be? I think, given their reproductive goals, it's obvious that their population dynamics hinge directly on how much livestock there is now, which establishes a kind of oscillatory stability between them. (See: the stable case of a linear autonomous ODE on R^2.) Thus, we have to think of eradicating this parasite as lifting a historical biological check on cattle populations in the Americas. With an already oversized cattle industry, is this a prudent choice for humanity to make? I don't think it is. We are already one of earth's all time most destructive, globally invasive species of all time. Everybody wants to build build build, and nobody wants to admit that we need a functioning biosphere to survive.

Author: @DaveC2729
Content: I'd question the term 'nuclear'. The type of radiation used for things like this doesn't necessarily have to be released from atomic nuclei--they could be using X-rays, which can be generated by non-nuclear processes (like your average medical X-ray for example, which is not nuclear.) Or, given how small these flies are, they might even be using higher-end ultraviolet radiation, like UV-B or C, and the owner of the last company I worked for bought a little LED light that put out UV-C when people still thought we could get rid of COVID. So I'd say it's highly probable that, while the process they use to sterilize the flies does involve ionizing radiation, it almost certainly isn't sourced from anything nuclear today and likely never was.

Author: @spookyonyx6
Content:
For anywone wondering if the same can be done to mosquitoes and wasps, the answer is: No*

Mosquitoes and wasps are absolutely vital to all the ecosystems they're a part of, first and foremost, most mosquitoes species have no interest in blood, but even the ones that do feed on blood have a special role in ecosystems, mosquitoes are the bulk of the foodchain, they're a significant part of the biomass in the ecosystems they're in, and as such, they feed a wide variety of small insectivores. Without them, competition between small insectivores would be far more intense, since no other insect has the same numbers as mosquitoes, and because of that, biodiversity would decrease everywhere, several species would be outcompeted, and the numbers of insects from other species would drop, leading to far less pollination and mass starving across all the foodchain, and all of this doesn't even consider their significant role in pollination, which they are absolutely vital for, and the ability of blood-sucking species to pass nutrients across trophic levels.

Also, wasps are efficient pest controllers, while spiders and mantises are good for controlling pests in closed areas like houses and forests, and while dragonflies are excellent at controlling pests near lakes, they both struggle to eliminate pests in open fields, for that, the wasps are by far the most efficient killers, they are not required to lay their eggs on lakes and they do not require closed spaces to ambush their prey, they just chase them down, and not only do they kill to feed themselves, but they also kill several insects to feed their larvae and queen, thus increasing their impact on pest population, and several species also parasitize the eggs of their targets, thus preventing them from even hatching, there's a reason why some species of wasp, like fairyflies, are sometimes dropped in crop fields to control pests, instead of dragonflies or spiders. And i didn't even mention the fact that several species are also stingless, that most wasps aren't nearly as temperamental as the most infamous species, like hornets and jackets, and that hundreds of species of plants, ranging from figs to orchids, can only be pollinated by wasps and nothing else, and that several more plants, like cabbages, have a symbiotic relationship with them.

However, not all wasps and mosquitoes are natural to the ecosystems they live in, for example, asian tiger mosquitoes, yellow fever mosquitoes, culex coronator mosquitoes, german yellowjackets, european hornets are all invasive outside of the old world (and are also the ones that torment people the most), and as such, they need to be exterminated from the lands they don't belong, and the same argument can be used for mosquitoes breeding near populated areas within their natural range, specially in areas of poverty and poor infrastructure., as to avoid the transmission of deadly diseases.

Content:
There is something that triggers me.
If you expose hundreds of of thousands flies to radiation, at one point you will have individuals that have a mutation enabling them to still be fertile. This is even more true if you keep breeding them from the same batch. 
So you will send flies (and among them the resistant ones) to territories that didn’t even know the specie. The resistant one will have enormous mating advantages, and will eventually replace the original population.
In other words, you’re creating a more resistant animal while wanting to eradicate it. And the process is unstoppable.
Maybe that we should have kept the flies on their natural habitat, without fighting them. It would have been cruel, but perhaps less damaging.

We had to change out of our regular clothes and put on what amounted to scrubs, then we put on hazmat suits and masks. No photos were allowed inside. The humidity was like nothing I’ve experienced before, and the smell was enough to almost make me cry. Our tour group barely lasted an hour in there. Everyone who works there must have stomachs of steel and way more courage than I ever could. I love insects and entomology, but I could never go there again. Very informative video as always!

Content: So, fighting flies with flies.

I can't imagine how this "war" can ever be won if we keep a live population reproduce and evolve freely in South America.

I mean, as long as we let (un)natural selection weed out the strains that can't fly over long distances, or breed some sort of infertility-resistance gene, it seems a given that we'll eventually lose our advantage and end up having to start all over again.

More importantly, this Panama-wall strategy looks a lot like a "let's take 'our' problem and make it 'their' problem". I don't see a strong incentive for the industry to invest the resources necessary to end it once and for all. Heck, if anything, I'm willing to bet some people would rather make sure the fight never ends at all if only so they can keep their business going.

(and that's even without discussing how going about it by trying to eradicate a whole species like it's a good idea in and by itself. You guys make a very compelling argument, and I do trust your jugement better than mine since I really didn't research anything into this so I'll take it as a given, but promoting that sort of idea still sound a bit weird to me)

All in all, I get that:
1/ there's a war out there with lives and the well-being of a lot of people and cattle beasts at stake
2/ right now we're at basically at a stalemate, with no clear sign that the powers-that-be really intend to go for the final push
3/ the more we wait, the more the enemy gets stronger until they eventually become able to tear through our defense
4/ ... okay, yeah... so you're saying we're screwed, right?

(note that I keep saying "we" and "our" even though I live in Europe, because from the look of it this stuff could very well end up migrating to the "old" continent, especially if it is already reaching Africa at a time where the game of ecosystems and dominant species has its cards periodically shuffled and dealt through climate change)

(oh dear, are we living at an interesting time or what?)

Author: @felipekid
Content:
This is a very informative video, but I noticed a significant gap in the information presented. Contrary to what was suggested, South America — especially Brazil, Uruguay, and Paraguay — has indeed implemented control initiatives against Cochliomyia hominivorax, including the Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) in specific regions.
In fact, Brazil partnered with COMEXA and neighboring countries in 2009 to release sterile flies along its southern border in an effort to control screwworm. There are also ongoing research and monitoring efforts in the Amazon and other affected areas, as the species continues to cause serious harm to livestock and public health.
It’s important to highlight these regional efforts so the global audience can have a more complete and balanced understanding of the issue.
Sources:
	•IAEA News Center: Status Report Released on the New World Screwworm in Latin America
	•MercoPress: “Sterile flies” to combat cattle screw worm in Uruguay
	•Agrociencia Uruguay: Historical perspective and new avenues to control the myiasis-causing fly Cochliomyia hominivorax in Uruguay

The larvae will grow a long head like appendage which reaches the surface of their hole to allow them to breathe while they eat the flesh. .
Bot flies do not actually need to deliver the eggs themselves some species will instead catch other insects such as mosquitoes and lay their eggs on them so that the mosquitoe will bring the eggs to the host.

.
Finally their is a species of bot fly that can Infect humans! It's called dermatobia hominus.
.
If you do get infected consult a doctor do not try and remove it your self as you may crush the larvae spewing it's guts inside flesh likely to cause infection of dangerous diseases.
.
The human bot fly is native to central and south America but no worry it only lives in the tropical and subtropical climates so you likely will never encounter one.

.
